Explanation
This three-year series of hymn selections was
roduced in order to systematically offer a
broad array of hymnody for congregations
employing the LSB one-year series of lessons
Several hymn lists were available to this
ompiler, each with its own peculiarities and
focus. Generally, the more a hymn was
represented among these lists, the more it
became represented in the three-year series
uch that a core of hymnody is used every
year, not least, the Hymn of the Day
A brief explanation of each list is in order:
Stuckwisch: Stuckwisch’s list is constructed
n order, opening hymn first, closing hymn
last. The Hymn of the Day is underlined here
and in all lists. Distribution hymns fall in
between and, occasionally, offering and post-
ommunion hymns are given (indicated by
“o”and “pc” respectively). The Hymn of the
Day is usually also his Catechetical Hymn of
the Week (else the catechetical hymn is noted
with “c”). The focus of the list overall is
atechetical, presenting a core of hymnody
with a fair bit of repetition of the best hymns
The list is LSB focused, employing many
hymns that were not available in TLH
Several of his choices seem rather
diosyncratic but are often quite clever. The
full list, including saints’ days, is available on
his blog: sword-in-hat. blogspot.com
Gehrke: This list comes from Gehrke’s
Planning the Service: A Workbook for Pastors
Organists, and Choirmasters. If opening or
losing hymns are suggested, they are placed
at the beginning or end, else most are just
aid to be on the theme of the day and are
listed below the Hymn of the Day. All
elections are from TLH, but LSB hymn
numbers are given where available. There are
many suggestions on the execution of
resenting hymns, especially the more
difficult ones: antiphonal singing, employing
the choir, etc
Reuning: In this list, Hymn(s) of the Day are
always noted first and then “auxiliary”
hymns. On Hymns of the Day, Reuning gives
ome deference to chorales used in Bach’s
antatas. Hymn choices are not limited to a
articular hymnal, so hymns only available
n TLH or LW are often given
Eckardt: This list comes from Eckardt’s The
Lutheran Propers with an Appendix of Hymns. It
s constructed in order of use as with
Stuckwisch. He gives separate lists for
ongregations using LSB or TLH. His
elections seem to be somewhat limited by
what is available in TLH, TLH remaining in
use at Kewanee. In Eckardt’s text are also
hymn selections for weekday masses and
about 40 hymns are appended in Section IV
This list is designed for yearly, recurrent use
LCMS: This section lists first hymn selections
ut out by the Synod for the Sundays in
n the order of use in the service: first hymn
Hymn of the Day, communion hymns, and
final hymn. After the gap are given any other
hymns employed in the Synod list for
Sundays in 2017, or after the penultimate
gap, hymns on the Gospel text from the LSB
Hymn Selection Guide that were not otherwise
listed, or after the final gap, hymns from TLH
Handbook associated with the Gospel text
(not otherwise listed)
ELS: This list is drawn from the Evangelical
Lutheran Hymnary (ELH)
SELK: HODs from their 2005 hymnal
Zion, Detroit: This list is given in order and
ncludes always an offering hymn. It is
unclear how much deviation there might be
from year to year in this list. The list from
3–2014 is offered here (see
ziondetroit.org). Choices are generally
nformed by Gehrke, and TLH is in use in the
ongregation, but hymns outside of TLH are
also used. Where a hymn’s stanzas may be
plit in use, the hymn is listed only once
Dietrich: The hymns in this section are for
atechetical use, a hymn suggested for
memorization each week
Judisch: These are Hymns of the Day
elected according to Dr. Judisch’s published
riteria
Thompson: In early versions of this project
Ludecus’s list 1589 was featured here from
Rev. Sean Daenzer’s translation at historic
lectionary.com. Mr. Matthew Carver has
rovided translations to many of these
hymns which were not otherwise available
(see Hymnoglypt matthaeusglyptes
blogspot.com or Walther’s Hymnal, referenced
n the following as “HG” and “WH”
respectively). Dr. Jason Thompson, however
ffers a comparison of de tempore hymn
assignments as Appendix 2 of his doctoral
dissertation which includes Ludecus and
twelve other 16 century lists. Hymns are
arranged in order of use in the service. Introit
hymns are noted with an “i,” postlude hymns
with a “p.” All other hymns are Graduallieder
r are indicated for use with the sermon and
are arranged according to frequency of
appearance among the lists. Those
represented in three or more lists are
underlined
Gerhardt: These are Paul Gerhardt’s
elections for Sundays and feasts from among
his hymns in a 1723 collection. Search “P
Gerhardi geistreiche Hauss- und Kirchen-
Lieder, nach des seel. Autoris” in Google
Books for the source
Carpzov: Hymns upon which he preached
Liliencron: These are Hymns of the Day
according to a de tempore hymn plan of
Liliencron, circa 1700. The list may be found
n Paul Graff, Geschichte der Auflösung der
alten gottesdienstlichen Formen in der
evangelischen Kirche Deutschlands
Bach: This list is derived from the chorales
used in Bach’s Sunday and festival cantatas
Stanzas are noted in superscript
Stiller: This list gives Günther Stiller’s
ummary of the Leipzig, Weißenfels, and
Dresden hymn schedules around the time of
Bach’s service in Leipzig. Hymns noted as
being composed for the Sunday are given in
talics. See pages 230 to 254 in Johann Sebastian
Bach and Liturgical Life in Leipzig
Years A, B, and C: In these lists the compiler
attempts to follow primarily and respectively
Stuckwisch and the LSB Hymnal Committee;
Gehrke and Zion, Detroit; and Reuning and
early Lutheran assignments, but there is
always a degree of interpenetration to
establish the core hymnody across years
Distribution hymns are given with the
number of musical systems noted in
uperscript. Such is a better indication of
length than the number of stanzas. Enough
distribution hymns are given to approximate
systems of music sung. Any Sequence
Hymn is noted with an “s” before the Hymn
f the Day. LSB is generally favored. Some
are was taken to distribute more difficult
hymns across years
